label: Person
name: Ivar Bårdsson
summary:
Ívar Bárðarson was a 14th-century Norwegian clergyman and the most important eyewitness reporter of the final decades of Norse Greenland's Western Settlement. After the death of the bishop of Gardar, he became the Catholic Church's official representative in Greenland — effectively the last institutional link between Norse Greenland and Europe before the colonies' mysterious disappearance.

Bárðarson arrived in Greenland around 1341 and compiled a detailed description of the Norse settlements, their churches, farms, and geography. His account — preserved in later Danish translations — describes the Western Settlement as already abandoned when he visited: 'nothing but wild cattle and sheep and no people there, either Christian or heathen.' This is one of the most evocative passages in the history of the Norse Greenland colonies, capturing the moment of their disappearance. His reports provide the primary primary-source evidence for the geography and economy of Norse Greenland before its collapse.

The disappearance of the Western Settlement (c. 1340–1360) that Bárðarson documented remains one of medieval history's most discussed mysteries. Modern scholarship attributes it to a combination of climate cooling (the onset of the Little Ice Age), economic marginalization as European trade shifted away from luxury Arctic goods, and possible conflict with or assimilation into Inuit communities. Bárðarson's account, though filtered through later recollection, is irreplaceable as the nearest contemporary witness to the end of Europe's most remote medieval colony.
